description: Lulo Patojo es un equipo apasionado por la tecnología, la innovación y los retos espaciales, que combina la berraquera y el ingenio para resolver problemas complejos a otro nivel. Estamos enfocados en un emocionante reto de ingeniería lunar, diseñando soluciones inteligentes orientadas a descifrar cómo lograr un aterrizaje exitoso y seguro en la superficie de la Luna.
summary:
What we developed: LUNARIS is an open web app that compares four lunar south pole sites over any dates from 2026 to 2030 by solar illumination and potential Earth visibility. It shows a 3D view of the south pole, timelines, a horizon view from each site and a side-by-side comparison.

How it addresses the challenge: Near the pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so ridges near and far decide whether a site is lit. LUNARIS precomputes the apparent positions of the Sun and the Earth every 10 minutes with NASA NAIF SPICE and JPL's DE440 ephemeris, and each site's terrain horizon from NASA LRO LOLA elevation models out to 300 km. We checked the method against JPL Horizons, published studies and NASA's illumination maps, and we publish the checks that miss too.

Why it matters: South pole missions need sunlight for power and the Earth in view for direct communication, and their dates often change. Long-term maps average over 18.6 years; LUNARIS answers for the mission's own dates, in under a minute, free and with no login, for mission planners, researchers and educators.
details:
What it does. LUNARIS answers one question in under a minute: which lunar south pole site has better solar illumination and Earth visibility during the period I choose? A user picks two to four of the four sites (Shackleton rim, LOLA Site 04; de Gerlache rim, LOLA Site 11; Malapert massif, LOLA Site 23; and Haworth, an Artemis III candidate region) and any dates between 2026-01-01 and 2030-12-31 (UTC). The page then shows:

- a 3D view of the south pole (Cesium Moon Terrain), with each selected site coloured by the share of the Sun visible at the time cursor; when the 3D view cannot load, a 2D LOLA map takes its place;

- timelines of the elevation of the Sun and the Earth against each site's terrain horizon, with bands that show when each is visible;

- a horizon view: the 360° terrain silhouette seen from each site, with the paths of the Sun and the Earth over the period, and, at the time cursor, how long until each one next sets or rises;

- a comparison table (mean illumination, sun time, longest shadow, Sun elevation range, Earth visible, longest Earth gap, Sun and Earth together, Earth any part), each metric with its definition and each site with its provenance: terrain layers, ephemeris, observer height, sampling and code version;

- a validation page with every check and its result.

The selected sites, dates and time cursor are stored in the URL, so a shared link reopens the same comparison.

How it works. An offline Python pipeline computes all the physics in advance, so the web app needs no backend:

1. Sun and Earth: NASA NAIF SPICE (through SpiceyPy) with JPL's DE440 ephemeris gives their apparent azimuth and elevation from each site every 10 minutes from 2026 to 2030, which is 262,944 samples per site.

2. Terrain horizon: for 3,600 directions (one every 0.1°), the highest terrain angle seen from 2 m above the ground, from nested NASA LRO LOLA elevation models: 5 m pixels up to 5 km from the site, 80 m up to 100 km and 240 m up to 300 km, with the Moon's curvature computed exactly.

3. Visible fractions: how much of the Sun's and the Earth's disks clears that horizon; eclipses by the Earth reduce the sunlight.

4. Static files: compact series, runs and horizons, tested and published with the web app on GitHub Pages. The browser slices the chosen dates and computes the metrics instantly.

The four analysis points come from one documented rule applied to NASA's long-term illumination maps (PGDA product 69): inside each region's 5 m map, at least 5 km from its edges, the 60 m cell that is sunlit most often, excluding permanent shadow and median slopes above 10°, then the highest 5 m pixel with a slope of 10° or less within 30 m of that cell.

How we checked it. The checks and their pass rules were fixed before the first validation run and never changed:

- Sun and Earth directions against JPL Horizons: largest difference 0.0018 arcseconds (limit 0.01). Pass.

- Regions of interest of Barker et al. (2021): all 8 points above 70% mean illumination. Pass.

- Points of Gläser et al. (2018): with the 5 m terrain the app uses, point S passes all three quantities; without the 5 m terrain (80 m and 240 m models only), 4 of 6 checks miss, and we publish that too.

- NASA PGDA illumination maps, a consistency check with no pass band and the observer at ground level like the maps: the share of time with any part of the Earth visible is within 1.8 percentage points of the Earth map. Our sun time reads lower than the Sun map (by up to 31.6 points, at Shackleton rim), as the plan expected, because 60 m maps cannot resolve such small, close relief.

Benefits. LUNARIS compares candidate sites for a specific mission window instead of long-term averages. It shows its sources and its checks, so its numbers can be checked and reproduced: the code is open source (Apache License 2.0), and the catalog, horizon, validation and map files record the commit of the code that produced them. It runs in any modern browser from a link, with no installation, login or backend. Over 2026–2030, for example, no site wins on everything: Shackleton rim gets the most sunlight (85.3% mean illumination), Malapert massif and de Gerlache rim see the Earth most often (57.6% and 57.3%, about tied), and de Gerlache rim has the Sun and the Earth together most often (48.2%).

What we hope to achieve. We want people who plan lunar missions to see visually how sunlight and Earth visibility change at each site during their own dates, so they can compare options quickly when plans change. We also hope teachers and students use it to understand why landing at the lunar south pole is so challenging. Next step: computing any point chosen by the user, on demand.

Limitations. Earth visibility is a geometric line of sight to the Earth's centre, not a radio link: antennas, scheduling and link budget are not modelled. The observer is fixed at 2 m above the ground. The data cover four sites, 2026–2030, in 10-minute steps, and the sites are analysis points chosen by a rule, not certified landing sites. The 3D shading is illustrative; every number comes from the LOLA horizon model.

Tools. Python 3.12 (SpiceyPy, NumPy, rasterio/GDAL, pydantic, pytest, Ruff, uv); TypeScript with React, Vite, Zustand, Apache ECharts and CesiumJS, with Cesium ion for the 3D terrain; GitHub Actions for tests and GitHub Pages for hosting. AI assistance: large language model assistants helped research documentation and draft code, documentation and slides; the team reviewed every change (README, "Use of AI").
